title: What is meant by “matters known through revelation”
text: Samʿiyyāt denotes matters whose establishment depends upon authoritative revealed communication, not simply anything audible. The division nevertheless begins with prophethood because the authority of that communication must be established. Rational arguments within this division are therefore not misplaced: they establish the messenger’s credibility, distinguish possibility from impossibility, and answer objections to the content transmitted. “The return” translates maʿād consistently; it includes the discussion of resurrection and the afterlife rather than a spatial journey back to a location.

title: Luṭf: gracious aid and a disputed obligation
text: “Gracious aid” renders luṭf without deciding the dispute in advance. The parties can agree that prophecy benefits human beings while disagreeing about whether divine wisdom makes its provision obligatory. The author’s final position denies the inference from beneficialness to a debt or obligation upon God; it does not deny that sending prophets is good. Read the ensuing objections together with this distinction, rather than treating every mention of luṭf as an endorsement of the Muʿtazilī principle.

title: Obligatory upon and necessary from
text: Wujūb ʿalayhi and wujūb ʿanhu cannot both be rendered simply “God must.” The former concerns an obligation attributed to the agent; the latter concerns an effect’s necessary proceeding from its principle. The philosophers’ appeal to providence aims to secure the ordering of the effect without an acquired purpose moving God to act. The theologians of Transoxiana are here reported as appealing to wisdom’s exclusion of foolishness. Al-Taftāzānī challenges that position as opening the same argumentative space as obligation upon God. This is his classification of the positions, not proof that all their proponents used identical formulations.

title: The benefits of prophecy do not imply that reason knows nothing
text: The list differentiates independent rational knowledge, uncertain judgement, and matters reason does not establish independently. A prophet may reinforce a truth already known, assist an incomplete rational inquiry, remove an uncertainty, or supply a route otherwise unavailable. The emendation “supporting reason” is therefore compelled by the local argument and by the later explicit parallel. The fear surrounding action and inaction is an objection about authorization to act within God’s dominion: it should not be turned into a medical or psychological claim about anxiety.

title: The dilemma about reason omits a third epistemic situation
text: The objection assumes that reason either endorses or rejects the prophetic teaching; the supplementary case then assigns undecided actions to practical need or precaution. title: A positive incapacity is not a mere absence of power
text: The apparently odd example of involuntary sitting must be retained. On the particular analysis being reported, ʿajz is a positive contrary relating to an existent act, not simply the privation of an ability to perform an absent act. If “incapacity to match the miracle” were taken in that technical sense, a matching act would have to occur involuntarily, defeating the intended sense. Muʿjiza therefore involves a further transfer in usage. This is an analysis of one technical account of incapacity, not the ordinary claim that an immobile person is incapable of remaining seated.

title: Why the definition begins with amr
text: Amr is deliberately broader than a positive physical action. It accommodates an occurrence such as water’s gushing forth and an omission such as fire’s not burning. Those who define a miracle as an act redescribe the latter as the production of safety or preservation of the body. “Event” is used here with that expressly extended sense; it must not exclude non-occurrence. The definition is also evidential: extraordinary character by itself does not establish a messenger’s claim.

title: Challenge and counter-performance

A sign could fail to authenticate the claimant because it belongs to someone else, predates the relevant claim, or explicitly contradicts him. The author then argues that a properly understood challenge already carries the required link. The minimum wording can simply identify what is to occur as the sign of truthfulness. No theatrical formula of challenge is required.

title: Why a claim to divinity is treated differently
text: The argument presupposes independent conclusive grounds excluding a human claimant’s divinity. An extraordinary event accompanying that claim cannot overturn those grounds and may count as a trial. A prophetic claim is not excluded in advance by the same reasoning, so an authenticating event has a different evidential setting. The passage is not saying that every impressive occurrence is an endorsement; its categories expressly allow occurrences that do not authenticate their recipient.

title: The date of a sign and the date at which it becomes evidence

title: The circularity objection

The author also recognizes the different route of independently excluding divine falsehood. These are alternatives, and the edition does not silently combine them into one argument.

title: Civil association and an agreed rule

title: Possessing a quality is not the same as conceiving it
text:
**Locator:** opening definition of kalām; `حصول الكيفيات النفسانية في النفس قد يكون بأعيانها ... وقد يكون بصورها`.

The generous person’s generosity and the ungenerous person’s conception of generosity illustrate two different ways in which something can be present to a soul. In the first, the person is qualified by the quality; in the second, the person understands what that quality is. Conceiving generosity does not make one generous. Correspondingly, conceiving a definition of a science does not amount to possessing the science’s many cognitions. The definition provides a comprehensive preliminary conception of what is to be acquired; study produces the relevant conceptions and assents themselves. Here “in their own reality” and “through their forms” must not be flattened into two synonymous expressions for having an idea.

title: Why defining a science precedes learning it
text:
**Locator:** opening; `صونا للطلب والنظر عن إخلال بما هو منها واشتغال بما ليس منها`.

The definition has a practical epistemic function: it prevents the investigator from overlooking what belongs to the science and spending the investigation on what does not. The author is not demanding that a beginner already know all the demonstrated conclusions. An overall conception can guide the acquisition of detailed knowledge without circularly presupposing that acquisition. The account also explains his acknowledgement that some disciplines were learned before an explicit textbook definition was customary: teaching can transmit questions and proofs without beginning with a formal definition of the discipline.

title: Kalām as actual cognition and as an acquired capacity
text:
**Locator:** opening, after the definition; `أو يكون ملكة تتعلق بها بحيث يكون عندهم ما يكفي في استحضارها`.

The commentary permits “knowledge” to designate either the relevant cognitions or the settled capacity by which a trained person can bring them to mind with the necessary resources. This is important when al-Ījī’s definition speaks of being able to establish doctrines. The theologian need not occurrently entertain every argument at every instant to possess the science. “Capacity” here is not a mere unrealized possibility available equally to everyone: it is an acquired disposition supported by learning and the ability to deploy proofs and answer objections.

title: “Religious doctrines” identifies a field, not an endorsement of every position in it
text:
**Locator:** opening; `سواء كان من الدين في الواقع ككلام أهل الحق أم لا ككلام المخالفين`.

The definition includes doctrinal claims presented as belonging to religion, including claims that the author considers false. The classificatory question “is this an exercise of kalām?” and the evaluative question “is this doctrine true?” are therefore distinct. A translation should preserve the author’s own contrast between the people he takes to be correct and their opponents, without turning the field-definition into an assertion that contradictory doctrines are all true.

title: The six divisions are ordered by explanatory dependence
text:
**Locator:** opening; `ووجه الترتيب توقف اللاحق على السابق في بعض البينات`.

The order is not merely an alphabetical or topical arrangement. Principles prepare the acquisition of knowledge; general matters supply concepts used across beings; accidents and substances provide more restricted inquiries; divine matters and revealed matters use results established earlier. Nevertheless, the author explicitly allows a question to be placed where its subject and argumentative usefulness make it most appropriate. Thus the vision of God can occur among divine matters, and restoration after nonexistence among revealed matters. A cross-reference should not be mistaken for an omission or a promise that the same material must appear twice in full.

title: Rational possibility and actual revelation answer different questions
text:
**Locator:** resurrection; `الحشر والإعادة أمر ممكن أخبر به الصادق فيكون واقعا`.

The argument has two components. First, the event is not demonstrated to be impossible. Second, a speaker already established as truthful reports that it will occur. Possibility alone does not establish occurrence; a report cannot establish an impossibility merely by being asserted. The earlier proof of prophetic truthfulness is therefore an indispensable premise, not an optional rhetorical embellishment. Translating samʿ simply as “hearing” obscures its role here as transmitted revelatory evidence.

title: Re-creation, reassembly, and restoration of life are not interchangeable descriptions
text:
**Locator:** resurrection, fourth investigation; `بإيجاد بعد الفناء أو بالجمع بعد تفرق الأجزاء`.

One account posits a period of nonexistence followed by renewed existence. Another posits surviving constituents whose arrangement and life are restored. In the cited position of Imām al-Ḥaramayn, both mechanisms are rationally admissible and no decisive transmitted proof selects one. “Suspension” must consequently not be translated as general scepticism about the afterlife.

title: Annihilation is not automatically a positive entity
text:
**Locator:** resurrection, third investigation; `بإعدام معدم أو بحدوث ضد أو بانتفاء شرط`.

The three proposed explanations are structurally different. Direct annihilation makes nonexistence the outcome of divine action without a created intermediary. A positive contrary introduces a purported existent called fanāʾ that excludes the body’s existence. Removal of a condition explains noncontinuance by the absence of what continued existence requires. Al-Taftāzānī’s criticism of fanāʾ as a positively existing contrary does not deny that things can cease to exist. Likewise, baqāʾ can refer either to persistence itself or, in a disputed theory, to a distinct condition or accident of persistence; those senses must be identified locally.

title: The accountability argument distinguishes personal identity from unchanged bodily attributes
text:
**Locator:** resurrection objections; `ولا يقال لمن جنى في الشباب فعوقب في المشيب إنها عقوبة لغير الجاني`.

The example concerns an offender whose age, appearance, and bodily constitution have changed. Such change does not by itself make subsequent punishment punishment of a different person. It is not a complete independent proof of any single metaphysics of the soul. The surrounding passage also appeals to original bodily parts, and the translation should not omit that qualification in favour of a purely disembodied account.

text:
**Locator:** questioning in the grave; `استبعادات لا تنفي الإمكان كسائر خوارق العادات`.

title: Deserving reward has more than one sense
text:
**Locator:** reward and punishment; `وأما الاستحقاق بمعنى ترتبهما على الأفعال والتروك ... فمما لا نزاع فيه`.

title: An occurrence can be certain without being a debt imposed upon God
text:
**Locator:** reward and punishment; `الوقوع البتة وهو لا يستلزم الوجوب على الله والاستحقاق من العبد`.

The inference under dispute moves from “this will certainly happen” to “God is under an obligation to make it happen.” Al-Taftāzānī denies that the former entails the latter. A divine promise can ground certainty of fulfilment without being explained as a creditor’s claim against God. The distinction is between grounds of necessity or certainty, not between reliable and unreliable divine speech. Translating both wujūb and unavoidable occurrence indiscriminately as “necessity” can conceal the point.

title: Cancellation and balancing are different accounts
text:
**Locator:** iḥbāṭ and muwāzana; `الأقل يسقط ولا يسقط من الأكثر شيئا` and `الأقل يسقط ويسقط من الأكثر ما يقابله`.

In the account attributed to Abū ʿAlī, the smaller quantity is cancelled while the larger remains undiminished. In the account attributed to Abū Hāshim, the smaller is cancelled and an equal amount is deducted from the larger. Thus one hundred units of punishment against one thousand of reward leave one thousand under the first model and nine hundred under the second. The numerical illustration is explanatory: it reproduces the formal distinction in the passage, not a claim that human beings can calculate a person’s final reward numerically.

title: A normative status need not act like a physical cause
text:
**Locator:** iḥbāṭ; `الاستحقاق اعتبار شرعي ليس له تأثير وتأثر حقيقي وفناء بعد وجود`.

This is a particularly important qualification of the preceding metaphysical objections. A status of entitlement can be a legally or revelatorily constituted consideration without being a concrete entity that efficiently destroys another entity. In that interpretation, cancellation means that God does not award the relevant reward; balancing means the corresponding non-award of reward and non-imposition of punishment. Arguments about simultaneous destruction, causal priority, and the coexistence of two annihilating causes may therefore miss their target. The author’s offering this reply should not be concealed merely because it weakens an objection associated with his own side.

text:
**Locator:** pardon; `من تحقق العفو في حقه يكون خارجا عن عموم اللفظ`.

The discussion consequently turns to the distinction between specifying a general statement and abrogating a report. text:

title: Approval can be qualified by an aspect
text:
**Locator:** intercession; `فإنه مرتضى من جهة الإيمان والعمل الصالح وإن كان مبغوضا من جهة المعصية`.

title: Repenting of one wrong while persisting in another

title: Assent, recognition, and submission: the disagreement has several levels
text:
**Locator:** faith; `المعتبر في الإيمان هو التصديق الاختياري` and the following five observations.

title: What counts as an explanatory expansion

title: Three objects of “for ever”
text: The objection moves among a command specifying an act, the continued force of that command, and divine knowledge of its duration. These must be separated. “Fast tomorrow” specifies the act’s time; a statement about whether the obligation remains in force concerns the normative predicate. Divine knowledge of an end does not by itself say that the recipients were told the end at the outset. The reply exploits these distinctions rather than granting that every temporally framed command constitutes an everlasting assertion of its own obligatoriness.

title: Wājib versus wujūb, with the scope made explicit
text: Al-wājib is the act required; al-wujūb is its being obligatory. A command whose object is “fasting for ever” does not automatically assert “its obligatoriness will itself remain for ever.” The author regards an explicit unqualified perpetuity of obligatoriness as incompatible with later cancellation, but allows a command’s object to have a long or indefinite duration while the command’s force has an endpoint known to God. His final refinement describes naskh as disclosure of that endpoint. This explains the reference back to the discussion of vision: the issue is the scope of a qualification, not eyesight as such.

title: Probabilistic reasoning in theology

title: The exact comparative question

title: Prostration as indication

title: Knowledge and teacherhood

title: The scope of al-ʿālamīn

title: Difficult obedience
